name: Bolivarian Socialism
summary: Bolivarian socialism is the Venezuelan current launched by Hugo Chavez, joining the nationalist and Latin American union ideals of Simon Bolivar with a 'socialism of the 21st century' of social property, nationalized strategic industries and oil-funded missions for the poor. It promises participatory and protagonistic democracy through referendums, recall and communal councils and communes, while building a strong presidency, a civic-military union and resistance to US imperialism and IMF-style policies. Critics describe its practice as state capitalism and increasingly authoritarian.
scope: The Chavista project as set out in the 1999 constitution, Chavez's 2005 turn to 21st-century socialism, and the 2013-2019 Plan de la Patria, with Maduro-era Madurismo treated as the continuation. Bolivarianism as a broader Latin American nationalism and later pragmatic factions (Delcismo) are not separately profiled. Doctrine is mostly about economy, democracy and sovereignty; many social and cultural questions are not addressed by it, so those answers are low confidence.

keyFigures.name: Hugo Chavez
keyFigures.role: Founder of the Bolivarian Revolution and architect of 21st-century socialism in Venezuela.

keyFigures.name: Simon Bolivar
keyFigures.role: Independence leader whose ideas of Latin American union give Bolivarianism its name.

keyFigures.name: Nicolas Maduro
keyFigures.role: Chavez's successor who led the hardline Madurista faction.

sources.title: Socialism of the 21st century
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Dieterich's framework, rejection of market economy and Soviet model, ALBA, nationalizations.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The constitution makes health a state responsibility with a public health system (Arts. 83-85), and Barrio Adentro delivered free clinics.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Chavista governments repeatedly raised the minimum wage as part of redistribution, though hyperinflation later eroded it.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Plan seeks to replace capitalist markets with grassroots control, and 21st-century socialism rejects market-economy principles.

public-ownership.rationale: Nationalization of oil and other key industries is a defining Chavista policy, and the constitution makes hydrocarbons state property.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Redistribution through oil money and social missions is central, but the sources stress oil revenue rather than taxing the rich.

unions-good.rationale: The constitution guarantees unions, bargaining and strikes (Arts. 95-97); Chavismo favors pro-worker organizing though it backed its own union federation against rival unions.

property-fundamental.rationale: Chávez accepted private property but promoted social property, and the constitution allows expropriation for the social interest.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Anti-neoliberal Chavismo imposed price, currency and supply controls and pushed distribution through state and communal channels against speculation.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare through the missions is a flagship achievement of the Bolivarian Revolution and the constitution defines a social state (Art. 2).

worker-ownership.rationale: The Plan promotes social, collective and workers' council forms of ownership and workplace participation, alongside state ownership.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Little documented in the sources on surveillance for terrorism; Chavista governments expanded security powers but also denounce US spying.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Not a Chavista theme; the constitution targets drug trafficking property (Art. 116) and government policy was prohibitionist, so a mild disagree is inferred.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The government passed laws against hatred in media (2017 Law against Hatred) which supporters defend, while critics call it censorship.

strong-leader.rationale: Chavismo is described as personalist and caudillo-style, and the 1999 constitution expanded presidential powers.

state-harmful.rationale: Chavismo builds a communal state and a strong social state; it is the opposite of anti-statism.

limit-guns.rationale: Government disarmament campaigns existed, but the sources say little about gun policy so this is a mild lean.

empower-police-military.rationale: The Plan stresses a civic-military union, a strengthened militia and domestic military industry; the military ran missions.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: The sources give no Chavista position on sex work; the constitution is silent.

decide-locally.rationale: Communal councils and communes take over state functions, but the project is steered nationally and centralizes oil income.

rehabilitation.rationale: The constitution (Art. 272) favors rehabilitative prisons, though not covered in the sources I read in detail; Chavista practice was punitive.

traditional-family.rationale: Constitution protects marriage and families, but Chavismo also stresses gender equality; no clear doctrine on traditional families.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: The constitution defines marriage between spouses and unions between a man and woman (Art. 77); Chávez-era government did not legalize same-sex marriage.

abortion-legal.rationale: Abortion remained largely criminalized under Chávez and Maduro; Chávez opposed liberalization, though some Chavistas disagree.

more-religion-public.rationale: Constitution guarantees religious freedom (Art. 59); Chávez used Christian language but clashed with the Church hierarchy.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The constitution recognizes indigenous peoples and the Plan speeds land titling; Chavismo frames itself as inclusive of the poor and Afro-descendants.

gender-social-construct.rationale: The sources say nothing on the theory of gender; the Plan commits to gender equality only in general terms.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Bolivarianism is described as nationalist-patriotic with a national ethic of patriotic service.

gradual-change.rationale: The project is explicitly a revolution deepened step by step but aiming at a point of no return, not respect for established institutions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Chavismo is not anti-immigrant; it ran mass naturalization and welcoming Latin American integration.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The Plan criticizes multilateral treaties limiting sovereignty and a pluri-polar world, favoring regional blocs over UN or IMF authority.

free-trade.rationale: Chavismo opposes neoliberalism and IMF/World Bank policy; ALBA was founded against the US-backed Free Trade Area of the Americas.

nation-first.rationale: Sovereignty is central, but the project pairs it with Latin American integration, so it rejects national selfishness while rejecting global governance.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: The Plan attacks imperialist interference and politicized human rights bodies, so interventions are viewed as imperialism.

open-borders.rationale: Gran Colombia union ideals favor regional unity, but nothing in the sources supports open borders globally.

limit-growth.rationale: The Plan doubles oil output while including an eco-socialist language; growth limits are not endorsed.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: The Plan frames an eco-socialist model and attacks carbon markets, but Venezuela's own oil expansion undercuts action.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: No stated position; the Plan mentions technological sovereignty but not technological optimism.

expand-nuclear.rationale: The sources do not discuss nuclear power; Chávez signed nuclear cooperation talk with Russia and Iran but nothing definitive.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Bolivarian Revolution is the project's own name and the Plan aims to pass the point of no return in the transition to socialism.

experts-over-public.rationale: Participatory and protagonistic democracy with popular control and social auditing puts the people over technocrats.

central-planning.rationale: The Second Socialist Plan is a state development plan with large investment targets, yet Chavismo rejects Soviet-style models and tolerates a mixed economy.

socialized-markets.rationale: Chavismo promotes social ownership and mixed forms alongside private firms; critics note the private sector produced about 70 percent of GDP in 2009.

land-value-tax.rationale: The sources never mention land taxation; the Plan handles land by eliminating latifundio, so the single-tax idea is simply outside its toolkit.

tax-inheritance.rationale: No explicit stance is documented; a redistributive anti-capitalist project fits heavy inheritance taxes.

basic-income.rationale: Missions give targeted aid and stipends, not an unconditional income; no documented position.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Economic self-sufficiency and food/industrial sovereignty are central aims, which point to protecting domestic production.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The Plan sets state targets for industrial parks, socially owned enterprises, refineries and oil output.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The Plan favors social property of strategic means but also family and cooperative property, so small ownership is accepted rather than central.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Chavismo is not communist in this sense; it talks of a post-rentier economy with continued wages and commune banks.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: The state keeps national power over the monetary system (Art. 156) and Chavismo wants public financial control.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: The Plan routes economic power through communes and workers' councils and state price controls, not through state-recognised employer-worker bodies, so a mild disagree is inferred.

one-party-rule.rationale: Chavismo claims participatory democracy with a dominant PSUV and allied parties, though critics say Maduro moved to one-party rule.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Bolivarianism descends from the republican independence tradition of Bolívar and rejects hereditary rule.

democracy-best.rationale: Chavismo presents itself as deepening democracy, though it also dismisses elite or foreign-influenced outcomes.

direct-votes.rationale: The constitution provides consultative, abrogatory and recall referendums (Arts. 70-74) and Bolivarianism stresses popular votes.

workers-councils.rationale: The Plan promotes workers' councils and communes to take over state functions, but the constitution retains parliament and a presidency.

right-to-secede.rationale: The constitution stresses territorial integrity (Art. 13) and nationalism.

natural-rulers.rationale: Bolivarian egalitarian populism rejects born elites, though it does elevate a charismatic leader.

political-violence-never.rationale: The movement began in a 1992 coup attempt and endorses armed civic-military defense of the revolution.

war-builds-character.rationale: The Plan calls Venezuelan military power defensive; no glorification of war is documented.

separate-church-state.rationale: The constitution guarantees religious freedom; Chavismo is secular in law but uses religious rhetoric.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The constitution is a secular document rooted in popular sovereignty and social justice.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The constitution assigns armed forces and public power to the state and the Plan wants a strong state security role.

military-superiority.rationale: The Plan calls Venezuelan military power defensive and deterring, not superior to rivals.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Chavismo is explicitly pluralist and recognizes indigenous peoples in the constitution (Arts. 119-125).

class-struggle-history.rationale: 21st-century socialism draws on Marxist ideas, though Chávez drew on Bolívar, Christianity and nationalist populism too.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Redistribution and the missions aim to cut inequality sharply; Chavismo does not pursue strict equal outcomes.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Constitution Arts. 119-120 recognize indigenous land rights and the Plan speeds land demarcation, though resource ownership stays with the state.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Anti-colonial and anti-imperialist rhetoric is strong, but reparations as such are not documented.

civilizational-union.rationale: Bolívar's union of Hispanic American countries and ALBA/CELAC are central; it is regional rather than religious.

self-interest-moral.rationale: 21st-century socialism opposes capitalist egoism and calls for solidarity and cooperative values.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The constitution lists many rights, but Bolivarianism stresses patriotic service duty; no clear priority.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The Plan's eco-socialist harmony between man and nature points this way, though the text is loosely stated.

limit-population.rationale: Neither the Plan nor the sources treat population control as a goal; a project that blames capitalism for poverty is inferred to disagree.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The Plan aims to industrialize and expand oil output despite eco-socialist language.

accelerate-technology.rationale: The Plan stresses technological sovereignty and domestic industry but says nothing about disruptive acceleration, so no direction is inferred.

human-enhancement.rationale: No source discusses enhancement and it has no link to Bolivarian themes, so the answer is a neutral placeholder.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Participatory popular power is the model; algorithmic government is not discussed.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: The government expanded surveillance and control of the internet; no explicit position on encryption.

restore-past-order.rationale: It claims a revolutionary future orientation, though it invokes Bolívar's legacy.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Chavismo is explicitly ideological (21st-century socialism), though critics note pragmatism under Maduro.

direct-action.rationale: Chavismo pairs popular mobilization with elections and a constitution, so it does not reject elections.

means-match-ends.rationale: Chavismo claims its participatory methods prefigure the communal state it wants, which suggests agreement, though the principle is never stated as such.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The Plan promotes industrialization, tractors, refineries and housing, plainly opposite to foraging.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: The Plan promotes industrial and agricultural expansion with specialised roles; abolition of the division of labour is a Marxist theme it does not take up.

distribute-by-need.rationale: 21st-century socialism seeks distribution to meet basic needs through missions and rationed food, though wages remain.

production-for-use.rationale: The Plan aims at social production and distribution against speculation, with continued state oil exports for revenue.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Dieterich's theory builds on labor value; Chavismo denounces capitalist exploitation, though it tolerates private firms.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Chávez said to reinvent socialism and avoid Soviet state socialism; the framework is electoral and gradual.

collective-farming.rationale: The Plan favors collective tractors and family, urban and indigenous farming as alternatives, a mix not a single collectivization.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Anti-imperialist discourse blames imperial domination for conflict.

taxation-theft.rationale: A social state relies on taxation (Art. 133 on duty to pay taxes) and Chavismo rejects libertarianism.

harm-principle.rationale: No documented stance; Chavismo is collectivist in outlook and restricts media.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The constitution recognizes collective rights of indigenous peoples (Arts. 119-125).

conscription.rationale: The constitution (Art. 134) imposes civic and military service duties, but practice is voluntary.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Bolivarianism is defined by popular participation, referendums and recall, which place voice and voting above exit.

state-as-business.rationale: The Plan treats the state as a social and communal provider, not a business.

positive-liberty.rationale: The constitution's social state and missions rest on providing material means as rights, in contrast to merely negative liberty.

media-academia-power.rationale: Chavismo accused private media of power and conspiring against it, as in the 2002 coup narrative, but less so universities.

hereditarian-race.rationale: The constitution bans discrimination (Art. 21) and Chavismo celebrates a mixed-race Bolivarian nation.

organic-representation.rationale: It proposes communal councils as new popular power, but alongside parties and elections.

total-state.rationale: Critics describe expanded state control, but the doctrine retains private property and a pluralist constitution.

national-rebirth.rationale: The Bolivarian Revolution frames itself as a refounding of the republic from a failed past.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The constitution bars cession of territory (Art. 13) and the doctrine is defensive and integrationist, not expansionist.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Critics note loyalty-based appointments, but ideology rejects feudal-style authority.

bound-labor.rationale: The Plan seeks to eliminate latifundios and give land to farmers, the opposite of bound labor.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The Plan calls for building a new moral, ethical and spiritual hegemony; no explicit epistemology is stated.

universal-morality.rationale: Chávez mixed Christian ethics, Bolívar and Marxism, and the sources give no position on knowable universal moral truths.

single-common-good.rationale: The Plan speaks of a collective national project, but socialist class framing recognizes conflicting interests.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Chavismo broke ties with Israel in 2009 and is pro-Palestinian, but the sources do not state a doctrine.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: The sources are silent on diaspora return; Venezuela's later large emigration makes the question awkward for the movement.

revive-national-language.rationale: The constitution recognizes indigenous languages as official for peoples (Art. 9) but Spanish is the main one.

workplace-democracy.rationale: The Plan promotes democratic workplace participation and workers' councils.

school-vouchers.rationale: The constitution makes education a free public service (Arts. 102-103) and Bolivarian schools expanded the public system.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Chavista governments ran heavy public spending, financed by oil and later by money creation.

economic-freedom.rationale: Chavismo opposes neoliberal economic freedom and accepted expropriations and price controls.

rule-by-example.rationale: Anti-corruption and patriotic ethic are valued, but laws and institutions also remain central.

national-self-determination.rationale: Latin American sovereignty and opposition to foreign domination are the central aim.

force-without-un.rationale: The Plan denounces imperial interventions and defends sovereignty, so unilateral force is rejected.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Chávez fused Christian and nationalist imagery with Marxism; no stress on reason alone.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Missions served residents broadly, including Colombian migrants.

work-for-welfare.rationale: The missions provided benefits as social rights, with no work test as a core feature.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Plan aims to replace capitalist relations with social property, rejecting a partnership with capital.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: A nationalist-patriotic movement that venerates Bolívar and national history would not sacrifice inherited institutions for novelty.

dominated-front.rationale: ALBA, UNASUR, CELAC and the BRICS alliance form a front of countries resisting Western domination.

workers-nation.rationale: Bolivarian socialism is patriotic and nationalist while seeking Latin American unity.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The constitution prohibits sex discrimination and recognizes housework (Arts. 21, 88).

ban-interest.rationale: The constitution regulates usury (Art. 114) but there is no ban on interest.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The constitution bans discrimination (Art. 21) and Bolivarianism presents itself as inclusive of the mixed-race poor, so segregation is flatly opposed.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The doctrine draws on Marxist ideas that the old state served elites and must be transformed into a communal state.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: The Plan sets a target of 6 million barrels a day by 2019 and new refineries and thermal plants.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Chavismo embraces plural cultures, though nothing on immigrant assimilation is documented.

elite-replacement.rationale: Chavista conspiracy rhetoric targets oligarchs and the US, not immigration plots, and the movement itself welcomed Latin American migrants.

proportional-representation.rationale: The constitution (Art. 63) guarantees proportional representation in elections, but the movement uses mixed systems favoring it.

national-mission.rationale: Bolivarian ideals are exported regionally through ALBA, but with respect for sovereignty.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The Plan commits to deepen gender equality and women's participation, without a structural theory.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Eliminating corruption and attacking the old political elites are central aims of Bolivarianism.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: The constitution protects equal rights and dignity; eugenics has no place.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Chavismo has demanded accountability for the Caracazo of 1989 but is itself accused of abuses.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The constitution establishes a social state with broad duties (Art. 2-3).

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: The constitution prohibits discrimination and Bolivarianism celebrates mixed heritage.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The constitution declares equality before the law and bans discrimination (Art. 21).

socialism-one-country.rationale: Chavismo builds socialism in Venezuela while promoting regional integration, without requiring revolution elsewhere.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Anti-imperialism leads to this view, but nothing specific is documented.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The constitution guarantees religious freedom but Chavismo had no stated view on religious personal law, which is not an issue in Venezuela.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The constitution guarantees freedom of religion and conscience (Arts. 59, 61), which a conversion ban would violate.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Not a Bolivarian aim; the Plan promotes livestock and agricultural output, so a slaughter ban is rejected.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The sources do not say; schools are public and religious freedom is protected.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: The Plan builds a stronger militia and defense against imperial threat, though not Leninist state theory.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The constitution places sovereignty in the people (Art. 5) and provides recall and referendums.

trade-surplus.rationale: No clear doctrine; oil exports dominate but the focus is self-sufficiency.

population-transfer.rationale: Equal rights and anti-discrimination in the constitution rule this out.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Chavismo rejects libertarian ethics and accepts revolution and militia defense.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: 21st-century socialism stresses solidarity and cooperation over competition.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Critics say the government used courts against opposition, but supporters give mixed positions.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The anti-imperialist focus on independence from foreign domination fits; no republican theory is cited.

separated-powers.rationale: The 1999 constitution adds citizen and electoral powers, but critics say the judiciary was made a tool; Chavismo is skeptical of checks on popular will.

vanguard-party.rationale: PSUV is a mass party, but Chávez emphasized popular movement over a disciplined vanguard.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The missions and Chávez's pro-poor programs are the movement's core purpose.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Mission Habitat built housing; no documented stance on right-to-buy.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The constitution guarantees the right to strike (Art. 97) and Chavismo is pro-labour, though it treated opposition-led strikes as sabotage.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: 21st-century socialism attributes poverty to capitalist social institutions.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The constitution is explicitly multiethnic and pluriculutural (Arts. 100, 119-125) and Bolivarianism celebrates a mixed people.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Elections and referendums are the democratic mechanism, not lotteries.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The constitution allows states of exception but critics say governments overused them.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Chavista governments fixed prices for essentials and fought hoarding (Art. 114 on speculation).

party-controls-media.rationale: The constitution forbids censorship (Art. 57), though critics say Chavista governments closed outlets and the state runs teleSUR.

party-commands-army.rationale: The Plan stresses a civic-military union, but the constitution places armed forces under the state.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Chavismo naturalized many migrants quickly; no documented wait.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Egalitarian socialist rhetoric about popular power points to agreement, but no pay rule for representatives is cited.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: The PSUV is an organized party but no doctrine of binding discipline is documented.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The Plan supports regional integration like ALBA and CELAC but criticizes treaties limiting sovereignty.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The president is commander-in-chief with extended powers under the 1999 constitution.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The sources contain no position on how a church should be governed; the constitution is neutral between religions.

clerical-rule.rationale: The constitution rests on popular sovereignty and secular law (Art. 5), so rule by religious scholars has no place.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Patriotism and defense of the Bolivarian homeland contradict revolutionary defeatism.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Constitution bans censorship; no moral censorship doctrine is documented.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Chavismo expanded presidential powers and lengthened the term, and Chavistas defended indefinite re-election as popular choice, as critics note.

recall-officials.rationale: Art. 72 provides recall referendums, and Chávez faced one in 2004.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Chavismo rejects US alliances and bases but builds its own alliances like ALBA.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Mission Habitat built housing for ownership, but a ban on renting is not documented.

people-in-arms.rationale: The Plan strengthens the National Bolivarian Militia and popular participation in national defence.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The Plan stresses agriculture and food sovereignty but no moral claim about rural life.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Gran Colombia and Bolívar's union of Hispanic American states are historic ideals.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The sources do not address this; Chavismo expanded universities for the poor but also attacked academic elites.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The constitution recognizes cultural diversity and indigenous cultures (Art. 121).

death-penalty.rationale: Art. 43 of the constitution states that no law shall provide for the death penalty.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: The Plan's gender equality commitment suggests support, though no curriculum is documented.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: A secular public school system with freedom of religion is inferred to teach evolution; nothing is stated on creationism.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Venezuelan sources I read say nothing on pornography, and the movement has no stated moral-censorship programme.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: The constitution grants citizenship by birth on the territory.

minority-language-support.rationale: Art. 9 and Arts. 121-123 recognize indigenous languages and cultures.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The constitution guarantees religious freedom (Art. 59) but nothing is said on exemptions from general law.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: A collective, patriotic movement has no stated view on eccentric ways of living.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: The Plan calls for eliminating international financial institutions' role in development, and ALBA opposes debt dependence.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Bolivarian sovereignty is explicitly economic as well as political, aiming at self-sufficiency and control of resources.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Chávez convened an elected constituent assembly in 1999 to write the constitution.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Chavismo claims to deepen rather than limit freedoms, though critics note repression.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The movement favors an equitable distribution of resources and Petrocaribe-style aid, though it prefers sovereignty over aid.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The Plan calls Venezuelan military power defensive and deterring and Venezuela has no nuclear programme, so own nuclear weapons are inferred to be rejected.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The president is directly elected under the 1999 constitution.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Chavismo brought the central bank under government direction, against neoliberal independence.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: The constitution forbids ceding territory (Art. 13), though not specific to peace deals.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Art. 115 allows expropriation for public benefit or social interest and Chávez promoted social property.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: The 21st-century socialism project criticizes the Soviet model as state socialism but gives no verdict of this form.

precautionary-principle.rationale: The constitution requires environmental impact studies (Art. 129).

collective-defense.rationale: The Plan builds ALBA and UNASUR but without a mutual-defense clause documented.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Anti-imperialist stance suggests so, but the sources do not discuss annexation.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The constitution guarantees religious freedom; no curbing of the Church is stated.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The 1999 constitution makes the president both head of state and head of government, and Chávez led his own party, so a non-partisan head of state is not the model.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Territorial integrity is a constitutional principle, and the movement is state nationalist.

region-keeps-system.rationale: The sources contain no position on one-country-two-systems arrangements; the movement favours a unitary-federal state with national economic control.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Bolivarianism is republican and rests on popular sovereignty, so a sacred or divine ruler is rejected.

flat-income-tax.rationale: A redistributive project built on social missions funded by the state would favour progressive taxation over a flat rate.

character-from-environment.rationale: Socialist outlook stresses social conditions and education in forming new citizens.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The constitution binds the president to law, although critics say it was not respected.

space-expansion.rationale: Space is not among the Plan's goals, which focus on food, housing, oil and social missions; a mild disagree is inferred.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The 1999 constitution centres popular sovereignty and a strong presidency, not balancing few and many.

leader-cult.rationale: Chavismo features portraits, slogans and mass praise for Chávez, and critics note caudillismo.

equal-parenting.rationale: Nothing in the sources addresses custody; the constitution's gender equality language gives no clear direction.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: 21st-century socialism has no stated doctrine on class struggle under socialism, and Chavismo frames itself as still in transition.

land-redistribution.rationale: The Plan aims to eliminate latifundio and land reform was a key Chávez policy.

refugee-return.rationale: The sources do not cover refugee return, so no direction can be inferred.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The constitution rejects territorial changes, though Venezuela claims Essequibo on historical grounds.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The constitution guarantees freedom of conscience and religion (Arts. 59, 61).

women-must-cover.rationale: The constitution guarantees equality and personal freedom (Art. 21), and a covering mandate has no basis in Bolivarianism.

common-currency.rationale: The Plan proposes the sucre ALBA currency and a regional bank.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Bolívar's union of Hispanic American peoples is central to Bolivarianism.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The constitution gives indigenous peoples cultural institutions (Arts. 119-124), but the general doctrine on national minorities is not stated.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The sources do not discuss minority emigration versus rights; no direction is inferred.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The doctrine fuses Marxist elements with nationalism and ethics, giving no clear materialist primacy.

ban-cartels.rationale: The constitution bans monopolies (Art. 113) and Chavismo attacks economic concentration.

no-bailouts.rationale: Nothing is documented on bailouts; a statist government would likely rescue strategic firms but also nationalise failing ones.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Critics say the judiciary was used for the government; supporters stress popular will.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: The Plan commits to women's participation but no quota is documented.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Self-sufficiency in food and goods is a central point, though it works within regional ties and not a closed colonial bloc.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: ALBA frames trade as solidarity with social aims, so binding standards fit its approach, though the sources do not discuss them.

moral-incentives.rationale: The Plan seeks a new moral and ethical hegemony and national ethic of service, reminiscent of Che's moral incentives.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Chávez's 1992 uprising was a military coup, but he later rejected the guerrilla foco model.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Republican Bolivarianism descends from an independence movement against colonial and hereditary hierarchy.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Bolivarian schools teach national and Latin American heroes with patriotic content.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Anti-imperialism rejects domination by purportedly advanced powers.

patriotic-education.rationale: Chavismo is nationalist-patriotic and has a national ethic of patriotic service.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Chavismo promotes affirmative recognition of indigenous and Afro-descendants.

public-money-creation.rationale: Government control of money and central bank under national power; no specific scheme documented.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Dieterich argues capitalism failed and a post-capitalist civilization is needed.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Bolivarianism is anti-imperial, so cultivating influence in former imperial regions is not an aim; its own regional integration is based on equality.

delink-world-market.rationale: The Plan wants to cut ties with imperial centres only to levels that keep independence, and builds ALBA, BRICS and Asian trade links, so it seeks a changed integration rather than a full break.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Anti-imperialist framing might support the idea, but the sources never state it.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The constitution bans discrimination (Art. 21) and an egalitarian project would reject a private right to discriminate.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The 1999 constitution has a detailed bill of rights, though Chavismo values popular power over judicial limits.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Anti-colonial stance supports it; no particular treaty doctrine is documented.

elective-rulers.rationale: The constitution has the president, deputies and officials directly elected and subject to recall, in a republic descended from Bolívar.

minority-veto.rationale: Majority-rule participatory democracy rejects individual vetoes.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Art. 350 of the constitution invokes the people's right to disown authority that violates democratic values.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The legislature is one of five powers, with a strong presidency.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: The sources do not address animal welfare, though the Plan's eco-socialist harmony with nature might sympathise.

animal-use-humane.rationale: The sources say nothing on animal use; the Plan's agriculture and eco-socialism sections give no direction.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Chavismo frames redistribution as justice, not charity from elites.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Bolivarianism calls for protagonistic participation of the people in public affairs, the opposite of withdrawal.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Chavismo accuses private media of serving elites and set up its own media, which suggests agreement, though no theory of mass culture is cited.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: The Plan seeks a new moral and spiritual hegemony, a Gramscian note.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: The Plan seeks to reduce ties with imperial centers that dominate; the anti-imperialist analysis holds that resources were extracted.

native-born-offices.rationale: The constitution reserves top offices to native Venezuelans (Art. 41), but not documented as doctrine.

party-own-road.rationale: Chávez said to reinvent socialism and not copy the Soviet or Cuban models.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Economic self-sufficiency is central, though Venezuela gave and took aid in ALBA.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Venezuela claims Essequibo, but this derives from state nationalism rather than doctrine.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: The constitution gives indigenous representation (Art. 125) but not leadership over others.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Chavismo is anti-fascist in rhetoric, but the sources give no view on constitutional founding values.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Chavismo is explicitly anti-fascist and anti-imperialist and would reject equating them.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: The question concerns US history that the sources never address.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Chavismo toppled colonial statues, such as Columbus, though not covered in the sources.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: The Plan commits to women's equality and says nothing on men's disadvantage.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: The Plan's gender-equality commitment points to prioritising violence against women, though no source states it.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: 21st-century socialism rejects imported Western models in favor of local forms such as communal councils.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The civic-military union gives the armed forces a political role in the revolution.

paid-care-work.rationale: Art. 88 recognizes housework as economic activity creating added value and entitles housewives to social security.

filial-duty.rationale: The constitution protects family duties of care but the sources contain no doctrine on adult children.

office-by-exam.rationale: The model is election, with critics noting loyalty appointments.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Chavismo nationalized strategic industries and opposes foreign domination of resources.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: The sources say nothing on divorce law; the constitution protects marriage but also spouses' equal rights.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Art. 72 recall and the commune model with accountable spokespeople.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: The constitution creates a public social security system (Art. 86) and Chavismo opposes neoliberal privatization.

land-use-tenure.rationale: The Plan favors social property over latifundio but also recognizes titled family farms.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The constitution gives the National Assembly budget approval.

single-official-language.rationale: Art. 9 recognizes indigenous languages as official for indigenous peoples.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Food and resource sovereignty and opposition to foreign domination suggest limits on foreign ownership, though land ownership by foreigners is not discussed.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: The sources contain no legal doctrine on disparate impact.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: 21st-century socialism critiques capitalist consumerism, though Chavismo pursued consumption through subsidized imports.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Critics claim ties with FARC but Chávez neither confirmed nor denied it.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: The Plan defends sovereignty and denounces imperial interventions.

corporate-influence.rationale: The movement attacks corporate power and neoliberal capture.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: The Plan targets imperial interference and Chavismo restricted foreign funding of NGOs.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: The Plan does not discuss demographic policy.

residents-only-property.rationale: The sources do not discuss local residency limits on property purchases.

job-guarantee.rationale: Art. 87 states a right to work and the state's duty to promote employment.

democratic-peace.rationale: The Plan sees democracy promotion by great powers as cover for imperialism, so the claim is inferred to be rejected.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Chavismo values lawful constitutional order, but invokes right of resistance.

non-intervention.rationale: Sovereignty and rejection of interference are central, though it supports ALBA solidarity.

industrial-unions.rationale: The constitution protects unions in general terms and the sources are silent on structure.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Anti-discrimination constitution; though Chavista rhetoric targets oligarchs, not ethnic minorities.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Art. 77 gives marriage constitutional protection, and an abolition proposal has no support in Bolivarianism.

public-access-to-information.rationale: The constitution gives a right to information (Art. 143), although practice was criticized.

local-production.rationale: Food sovereignty, local commune production and distribution chains are Plan aims that favour production near consumption.

informal-organisation.rationale: The Plan builds formal communes, councils, a militia and a mass party rather than small informal groups.

national-law-over-international.rationale: The Plan denounces multilateral bodies limiting sovereignty and attacks the Inter-American Commission.

religious-nation.rationale: The constitution is pluralist and secular, and Chavismo defines the nation by the people and Bolívar's legacy, not a shared religion.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Anti-imperialism opposes tribute and deference to dominant powers.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The Republic owns hydrocarbon wealth under Art. 12 and the movement redistributes oil income nationally.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Chávez accepted private property and aimed at social ownership of strategic means only.

defeat-communism.rationale: Chavismo allied with Cuba and the Communist Party of Venezuela.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Missions are state-run public services; mixed private provision is not favored.

religion-illusion.rationale: Chávez declared himself a Christian and used Christian symbols.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: 21st-century socialism views capitalism as failing, though some Marxist views grant its progress.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Plan links gender equality with the transition to socialism.

socialized-care.rationale: Art. 88 recognizes homework and the state supports childcare through missions.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Bolivarianism is nationalist but has no linguistic purism; the sources never mention it.

treaties-binding.rationale: Constitution recognizes indigenous rights, but treaties as such not discussed.

cooperative-communities.rationale: The Plan builds 3,000 communes with communal property and councils.

majority-settlement.rationale: Plan protects indigenous territories and constitution bans discrimination.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Chávez said to reinvent socialism beyond both capitalism and Soviet communism; in practice he allied with socialists.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Venezuela claims Essequibo on historical grounds, but the sources give no general doctrine on historical ties.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Holocaust denial is not part of any Chavista programme, though the sources do not discuss the issue.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Chavismo did not criminalise homosexuality and its egalitarian constitution bans discrimination.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Chavismo claims pluralism, though critics document repression.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The constitution guarantees freedom of religion and worship (Art. 59), which rules out punishing false religion.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The Plan denounces imperial domination and seeks sovereignty over resources, directly opposed to colonial exploitation.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: The question is about Islamic doctrine and has no bearing on Bolivarianism; Chavismo only allied politically with Muslim-majority states.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The constitution rests on popular sovereignty, not religious law, and bars religion as a test of legitimacy.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Bolivarianism is defined by participatory and protagonistic democracy and communal councils.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: The Plan is inclusive of women, indigenous and class concerns, but no theory of intersectionality.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: The sources report no Chavista legal recognition or opposition, and positions within the movement differ.

assisted-dying.rationale: Nothing in the sources addresses this and the constitution protects the right to life (Art. 43).

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Chavismo openly places itself on the socialist left and rejects third-way centrism.

alienated-labor.rationale: Mészáros and Lebowitz's analyses of alienation influenced Chávez.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Chavismo allies with Iran and other states and treats cultural clash narratives as imperial propaganda; the sources do not discuss the claim.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Art. 5 places sovereignty in the people, and the movement's legitimacy rests on elections and referendums.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: The constitution protects religious freedom but dress in state institutions is not covered.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Constitution protects workers' rights; not documented specifically.

social-market-economy.rationale: The project aims to replace capitalist markets rather than regulate them.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The Plan consolidates the civic-military union, the militia and a domestic arms industry, the opposite of abolition.

rich-first.rationale: Chavismo rejects trickle-down: redistribution and priority for the poor are its aims.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Chavismo is aligned with Russia, China, Cuba and Iran against the US.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The constitution fixes elected, recallable republican offices; dynasty has no place in Bolivarianism.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: The Plan includes commune banks, similar but not documented as interest-free.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Chavismo is defined by opposition to IMF and World Bank policies, and the Plan wants to remove their role from national development.

property-franchise.rationale: The constitution has universal suffrage and the movement draws its support from the poor.

domination-women-nature.rationale: The Plan's eco-socialism and gender equality hint at this, though not stated as connected.

reification.rationale: Mészáros and Lebowitz's Marxist analyses of alienation shaped Chávez, so the claim is consistent, but it is not stated in the sources.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Chavismo argued private media served oligarchic interests, justifying public media.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Critics note rule by decree under enabling laws, which Chavismo used often.

racial-franchise.rationale: Universal suffrage and a ban on racial discrimination are in the constitution (Art. 21).

online-participation.rationale: Participatory democracy supports more channels for citizens, but internet deliberation is not mentioned.

open-government-data.rationale: Constitution gives access to information, but not documented.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Art. 77 bases marriage on free consent and equal rights, and Art. 59 protects religious freedom.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Anti-discrimination principles in the constitution oppose targeting a religious minority.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Popular power and communal councils resemble citizen deliberation, though sortition is not used in the movement.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: The constitution is neutral on religious doctrine and the sources have no stance.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Anti-capitalism and attacks on oligarchic power imply concentrated wealth threatens popular rule.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Nothing in the sources addresses military service by gay people.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Chávez identified as Christian and the constitution protects religion, so atheist promotion is rejected.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: The Plan expands security forces and militia; abolition is a libertarian-left idea outside Chavismo.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The movement favours majority popular rule, so consociational power-sharing is inferred to be disliked.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The missions are state-run social programmes funded by oil revenue, an explicit choice of state action over charity.

term-limits.rationale: Chavismo expanded presidential powers and lengthened the term, and critics note it extended re-election, which cuts against term limits.

vote-delegation.rationale: Liquid delegation is not mentioned; the movement uses recall and referendums instead.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Not discussed in any source and unrelated to Bolivarian priorities.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Chavismo has no doctrine about religious office; the constitution leaves it to religions.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Art. 77 bases marriage on the equal rights and duties of spouses.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Constitution allows foreign residents vote in local elections (Art. 64) under conditions.

rent-control.rationale: Chavismo's housing policy and price controls included rent regulation.

abolish-ip.rationale: Nothing in the sources addresses patents; Chavismo stresses technological sovereignty.

uniformed-youth.rationale: The Plan talks of popular participation in defence, but uniformed youth movements are not mentioned.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: No nuclear weapons on the territory; not documented as doctrine.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Art. 13 of the constitution prohibits foreign military bases on Venezuelan territory.

recognise-genocide.rationale: The sources do not address genocide recognition.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Dieterich's equivalent economy rests on the labour theory of value and rewarding value-creating work.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The militia and civic-military defense accept armed defense.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Bolivarianism stresses continuity with Bolívar's independence project, but no claim of ancient unbroken identity is documented.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: No Chavista position on the construction of sex is documented.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: No Chavista position on feminist theory is documented; the Plan speaks of women as a group.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Bolivarian patriotism venerates Bolívar and the heroes of independence and revolution as models of service.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The Plan speaks of a moral, ethical and spiritual hegemony, but Chavismo does not frame politics as good versus evil theology.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: The sources are silent on diaspora homelands.

culture-before-state.rationale: Chavismo uses state power (missions, communes, plans) to drive cultural change, so state building comes first.

god-not-male.rationale: Nothing in the sources addresses theology of gender.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Nothing in the sources addresses this.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The movement is class-based and pluralist, so ethnic ownership is inferred to be rejected.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: No source addresses ethnic territorial mergers.

independent-unions.rationale: The government backed its own union federation against opposition, but the constitution permits independent unions.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The Plan returns power to the people through communes and workers' councils.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Water, hospitals and clinics belong to the state in the missions and nationalised services of the Revolution.

second-chamber.rationale: The 1999 constitution abolished the Senate, creating a unicameral National Assembly.

municipal-property.rationale: The Plan favors communal property but also state ownership of strategic means.

confederal-coordination.rationale: The Plan builds communes federated into communal cities, though national direction remains strong.

family-wage.rationale: Art. 91 guarantees a wage sufficient to live with dignity and cover basic needs of the family.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: The sources do not discuss drug regulation.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Currency and capital controls favor state oversight of money.

online-anonymity.rationale: Government censorship of online media; not stated as doctrine.

person-over-state.rationale: The constitution values human dignity, but collective interest weighs heavily.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The Plan seeks a moral, ethical and spiritual hegemony, implying politics should serve more than material life.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Venezuelan federalism is in practice strongly centralised and the national assembly holds power over regions, though this is not discussed.

gm-crops.rationale: Chavista government banned GM seeds in 2004 under food sovereignty, though not in the sources I read.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Chavismo organises by class and the people as a whole and the constitution prohibits racial discrimination.

racial-pride.rationale: The sources contain no stance; Chavismo celebrates a mixed Venezuelan identity and indigenous and Afro-descendant recognition.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: The Plan calls Venezuela's military power defensive and deterring.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Bolivarian union is by shared Hispanic American history more than language.

communal-electorates.rationale: Universal and direct suffrage under the constitution leaves no room for separate religious electorates.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Chavismo alleges US plots against Venezuela and allied governments.

free-public-college.rationale: Art. 103 makes public education free through undergraduate level.

pollution-taxes.rationale: The Plan rejects carbon markets but the sources do not mention pollution taxes.

future-generations.rationale: Art. 127 binds present generations to environmental protection.

women-distinct-values.rationale: The sources give no position on women's distinct values.

arms-reduction.rationale: The Plan expands the military and militia and builds a domestic arms industry, so lower armaments are not a goal.

open-diplomacy.rationale: The sources are silent on secret agreements.

capital-controls.rationale: Chavista governments imposed currency and capital controls as part of their anti-neoliberal economic policy.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Chavismo built a popular militia and tolerated armed colectivos, which cuts against a strict state arms monopoly.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The Plan builds up the military and militia for defence, so refusal of orders is not endorsed.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Art. 96 guarantees the right to collective bargaining.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Not documented; the movement prefers missions and wage rises to tax credits.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Chavista governments financed missions with oil revenue and large deficits and rejected neoliberal limits.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: The Plan calls for a pluri-polar world and new financial architecture of ALBA.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Communal state aims to replace the old state, though via constitution.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The Plan sets out a specific socialist blueprint with social property and communes, so open experiment is not its approach.

nature-as-capital.rationale: The Plan calls for dismantling carbon markets and an eco-socialist harmony with nature, against pricing ecosystems.

sacred-nation.rationale: Bolivarianism is nationalist-patriotic, but sacralising the nation is not documented.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Education is free under the constitution, so student debt is not a Venezuelan issue.

internal-colonialism.rationale: The sources do not address regional exploitation within states.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Not addressed, though socialist aims to create a new humanity might disagree.

public-service-media.rationale: Chavismo built state media like teleSUR, but they are not independent of government.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Chavismo has no stated doctrine on comparative religion.

farm-price-support.rationale: The Plan promotes farm support, cooperatives and public food distribution.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Venezuela has no nuclear weapons and the sources do not address the question.

workers-own-party.rationale: PSUV and its allies claim to be a party of the working people.

ban-fgm.rationale: The sources do not discuss FGM, though a ban would fit the equality commitments.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Art. 21 bans sex discrimination and Art. 88 guarantees equal treatment in work and home labour.

one-language-many-names.rationale: The sources are silent on language naming disputes.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: The constitution relies on state environmental duties (Arts. 127-129), not private liability.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: The constitution recognizes indigenous customary law and authority (Art. 260).

environment-over-liberty.rationale: The Plan favours an eco-socialist model but the sources give no priority rule.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: The sources do not address sentencing law.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: The sources do not address immigrant language requirements.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: A pro-labour movement is inferred to oppose the right-to-work approach, though not discussed.

voter-id.rationale: The sources do not discuss voter identification; Venezuela already uses biometric identification.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Art. 59 guarantees religious freedom to all faiths and the state has no established religion.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Chavismo defends deeper participatory democracy, not just procedure.

premarital-sex.rationale: Chavismo has no stated moral doctrine on this issue.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Critics report censorship, but the movement has no stated doctrine on shutdowns.

negative-income-tax.rationale: The Chavista approach is state missions and public services rather than a means-tested cash payment.

women-suffrage.rationale: Art. 21 bans sex discrimination and the constitution has universal suffrage.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Chávez was a professed Christian and Chavismo does not criticise religion in this way.

race-social-construct.rationale: The constitution's anti-discrimination and mixed-people framing is consistent with this, but it is not stated.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Venezuela created a women's ministry and the Plan commits to equality.

homestead-ownership.rationale: The Plan seeks to eliminate private latifundio and put land in social ownership.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: The Plan criticizes human rights bodies and politicized courts.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Not addressed; the state is secular though Chávez was personally Christian.

gendered-self-government.rationale: The Plan stresses women's participation and the constitution recognises indigenous self-government, so combining them is consistent.

defend-planned-state.rationale: The Plan defends the revolution against imperial attack, with Cuba as ally.

indirect-election.rationale: The president and assembly are directly elected, and communal councils are meant to add to rather than replace direct votes.

national-church-status.rationale: The constitution gives no church special status.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: The sources do not address ethnic territorial autonomy beyond indigenous rights.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Venezuela claims Essequibo and rejects arbitration, so a plebiscite is unlikely to be endorsed, but no doctrine is documented.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Bolívar's tradition of uti possidetis and Venezuela's own territorial claims suggest keeping inherited borders, though not stated in the sources.

simple-living.rationale: The sources do not take a position, though anti-consumerist themes exist.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: The constitution protects indigenous habitats and land rights (Arts. 119-120) and the Plan titles indigenous lands, but restricting outside settlement is not stated; leaning on that protection gives no firm answer.

equal-conscription.rationale: The constitution (Art. 134) states civic duties for all but the sources say nothing on gender parity.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: A nationalist-patriotic movement venerating Bolívar is inferred to endorse a bond with the ancestors' land.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Art. 43 protects life and the constitution requires due process, which rule out killings without trial.

close-ties-china.rationale: The Plan seeks closer ties with Asia and alliances with BRICS.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: The sources do not address kin minorities abroad, though Venezuela's emigrant community is large.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Art. 12 makes mineral and hydrocarbon deposits property of the Republic, held for all, though compensation to individuals is not mentioned.

self-ownership.rationale: Marxist-influenced collectivism cuts against strong self-ownership, but the sources say nothing on it.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: The sources do not discuss consumption taxes.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Missions are universal public services aimed at the poor in poor areas, not means-tested transfers.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Chavismo built the PSUV and communal bodies; the sources describe a party movement, not bypassing of mediators.

no-business-privileges.rationale: The constitution bans monopolies (Art. 113) and Chavismo attacks oligarchic business, so ending special privileges is consistent.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: The constitution is neutral and Venezuela has no confessional politics, so the issue does not arise.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: The Plan stresses industrial modernisation and indigenous respect, but the sources do not combine them.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Art. 77 treats spouses as equal, so wife-initiated divorce is consistent, though not discussed.

national-resource-control.rationale: Art. 12 makes hydrocarbons property of the Republic and the Plan insists on national control.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Twenty-first-century socialism and the Plan de la Patria aim at redistributing wealth and social justice by the state, so an adherent rejects judging fairness by process alone.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; inferred from Chavismo's opposition to international financial institutions and support for redistribution.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Chavismo stresses the rights of Afro-descendant and indigenous people and treats racial inequality as continuing; inferred, as the sources do not discuss this claim directly.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: The 1999 constitution allows citizens to disown authority that violates democratic values and rights; the natural-law claim itself is inferred.

automate-paid-work.rationale: The Plan stresses work and communal production, while 21st-century socialism also talks of freeing people from alienated labour; adherents have no clear line, so this is inferred.

multipolar-world.rationale: The Plan de la Patria and Chavista foreign policy call for a multipolar world against US dominance, and ALBA and regional blocs serve that aim.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Twenty-first-century socialism draws on Marxist political economy, which holds that labour creates value.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Bolivarian nationalism links love of country and Bolivar's legacy with serving the poor majority, which is the core of Chavismo.

material-over-identity.rationale: Chavismo mixes class politics with the rights of women, Afro-descendants and indigenous people, so it would not confine the left to material interests; inferred.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: The Plan envisages a mixed economy with a leading role for the state and the ruling PSUV; the statement is framed on the Chinese model, so this is inferred.

missingStatements.text: Citizens should be able to vote to recall a president in the middle of the term.
missingStatements.rationale: The 1999 constitution provides recall referendums for all elected officials, and Chávez submitted to one in 2004.

missingStatements.text: Poor countries should form regional blocs to trade and finance each other outside the control of the United States and international financial institutions.
missingStatements.rationale: The Plan sets out ALBA, UNASUR, CELAC, Petrocaribe, the sucre currency and an ALBA bank to reduce dependence on imperial centres.

missingStatements.text: Armed civilians should be organised into a popular militia that takes part in national defence alongside the army.
missingStatements.rationale: The Plan calls for the civic-military union and strengthening the National Bolivarian Militia.

notes: Practice diverged from doctrine: critics report media closures, politicised courts, and de facto dollarisation and courting of private capital under Madurismo and Delcismo. Wikipedia-derived sources dominate because open-access primary texts on 21st-century socialism could not be fetched; the constitution is the primary source.
